Measure No: 20-388
Caption:Licensure of Large Retailers to Finance a Clean Energy Fund
Question: Shall voters adopt ordinance imposing on large retailers a licensing requirement and 2% fee to finance a
clean energy fund?
Summary: The proposed ordinance would amend the Eugene code to, beginning January 1, 2029, require large retailers
to obtain a license and pay an annual 2% license fee on gross profits from retail sales within the City. The
ordinance defines “large retailer” as one engaged in retail sales in Eugene with gross profits exceeding
$1,000,000,000 nationally and $500,000 in Eugene, excluding contractors, utilities, cooperatives, and credit
unions. Gross profits from retail sales upon which the 2% is calculated would not include sales of most
groceries, medicines, residential garbage and recycling services, and health care services. The proposed
ordinance would require proceeds from the license fee to be placed in a “Eugene Clean Energy Fund”
dedicated to funding renewable energy and energy efficiency programs; clean energy job training,
apprenticeships, and contractor support; green infrastructure programs; future innovation; and fund
administration (not to exceed 10% starting in 2030). The ordinance would require an expert committee to
recommend use of funds, evaluate effectiveness of fund, and ensure work funded is performed by historically
disadvantaged groups.

Ballot Title
Caption: Amend Corvallis Charter to change city council,
wards, and terms
Question: Shall City amend charter to change number of
councilors and wards, length and staggering of terms, and
impose term limits?
Summary: This measure would amend the City's existing
home rule charter. The Oregon Constitution gives city
voters the right to adopt and amend charters. Charters grant
legal authority to cities, describe a city's form of government,
and assign duties to city officials.
If approved, this measure would amend sections 8, 9, and 10
of the current charter to change the number of city councilors
and wards from nine to six, change councilor terms of office
from two to four years with staggered elections, impose term
limits of three consecutive terms for councilors and the
mayor, and make other related changes. No other sections of
the Charter would be changed by this measure.
This measure was referred to the voters by the City Council
based on the recommendation of the City's Charter Review
Task Force.
Explanatory Statement
If approved, this measure would amend the City’s current
charter.
The proposed charter amendments are based on the
unanimous recommendation of the City’s Charter Review Task
Force. The Task Force included the following individuals:
Charles Maughan (Mayor)
Briae Lewis (City Councilor)
Jan Napack (City Councilor)
Ava Olson (City Councilor)
Danielle Chambers (Community-at-Large)
Steve Lee (Community-at-Large)
Shelley Ries (Community-at-Large)
The City Council approved submitting this measure to the
voters.
The Oregon Constitution gives city voters the right to adopt
and amend home rule charters. A charter grants legal
authority to a city government, describes the city’s form of
government, and defines the roles and responsibilities of city
officials.
This measure would make several changes to sections of the
City charter relating to the City’s form of government.
Specifically, this measure would amend the following sections
of the charter:
Section 8, relating to the City Council. This section would be
amended in the following ways:
• Changes the number of councilors from nine to six.
• Changes the term of office of councilors from two years
to four years.
• Staggers the elections of councilors such that councilors
from even-numbered wards are elected in federal
presidential election years and councilors from odd-
numbered wards are elected in federal midterm election
years.
• Imposes term limits on councilors. A person could not
serve more than three consecutive terms as a councilor,
regardless of ward. Partial terms of less than two years
would not be counted. Terms served prior to January
2027 would also not be counted.
• Describes how the transition from the current Council
structure would occur though an election of all six
councilors in November 2028, where councilors from
odd-numbered wards would serve an initial two-year
(rather than four-year) term in order to obtain the
staggering of terms described above.
• Makes other revisions for clarity.
Section 9, relating to wards. This section would be amended in
the following ways:
• Changes the number of wards from nine to six.
• Requires City Council to make its initial designation of
the six wards no later than December 31, 2027.
• Removes existing language providing a 25-day period of
time during which Council can designate wards.
• Removes language regarding revision of wards.
Section 10, relating to the office of mayor. This section would
be amended in the following ways:
• Clarifies that the mayor is elected from the city at large.
• Removes language relating to the initial election of a
mayor in 1954 and replaces it with language providing
that the mayor is elected in federal midterm election
years, which aligns with the current election schedule.
• Imposes term limits on the mayor. A person could not
serve more than three consecutive terms as mayor.
Partial terms of less than two years would not be
counted. Terms served prior to January 2027 would also
not be counted.
• Makes other revisions for clarity.
No other provisions of the Charter would be changed by this
measure.
The full text of the proposed amendments and task force
report are available at
https://www.corvallisoregon.gov/cm/page/november-2026-
election-ballot-measure.
(Submitted by City of Corvallis)

arguments.text:
THE RESPONSIBLE STEP FOR A COMMUNITY I LOVE
I care deeply about Corvallis—our downtown, our
neighborhoods, our local businesses, Oregon State University,
and most importantly, the people who choose to call this
community home.
I don’t consider myself particularly political, and I don’t look at
Measure 2-159 through a political lens. To me, this is about
something much simpler: Are we giving the people we elect the
best structure possible to make thoughtful, responsible
decisions for Corvallis?
I believe we can—and must—do better. Not by pointing fingers,
but by giving the people willing to serve our community a better
system for doing the work.
Our City Council is asked to make increasingly complicated
decisions about housing, public safety, infrastructure,
transportation, land use, economic vitality, and our City’s
financial future. These decisions can affect Corvallis for
decades, yet our councilors currently serve just two-year terms.
Four-year terms provide more time to learn, build relationships,
tackle difficult issues, follow through on important work, and
ultimately be accountable for the results.
Staggered elections provide continuity, ensuring experienced
councilors remain as new members join. Six wards maintain the
geographic representation Corvallis values while creating a
more focused governing body. And reasonable term limits value
experience while still making room for new people, new energy,
and new ideas.
What I appreciate about this measure is its balance. It isn’t
about one candidate, one City Council, one election, or one
political viewpoint. The structure we choose today will serve
Corvallis regardless of who holds office tomorrow.
I’ve always believed strong communities don’t happen by
accident. They happen when people care, participate, invest in
their community, listen to one another, and make responsible
decisions with the long term in mind.
Corvallis is worth that kind of thinking.
I believe Measure 2-159 is a thoughtful, balanced, and
responsible step toward better local government.
Please join me in voting YES on Measure 2-159.
Lee Eckroth

Vote No on Measure 2-159
Measure 2-159 asks Corvallis voters to change multiple City
Charter sections and multiple City practices with one vote, yes
or no, as if all changes are equally impactful, reasonable and
time-critical. They are not.
First, placing term limits upon the mayor and city councilors
removes choice by voters. While a reasonable person may
consider an elected City official holding an office for more than
12 years to be excessive, long-term knowledge and experience
are every bit as important on Council as high-energy
inexperience of newly elected officials. We need both, and that
is a decision for voters at each election. Mandating term limits
mandates limited voter power. This change alone should result
in a NO vote.
Second, removing the clauses about when the city council may
redraw ward boundaries after 2027 and about protecting the
one-person, one vote principle invites opportunities for future
City Councilors to create favorable chances for certain councilor
candidates. If the current City Charter wording is unreasonable,
that is no reason to remove ALL Charter guidance on the timing
of ward changes after 2027.
Third, changing the number of wards and ward councilors to an
even number increases the already significant powers of the
mayor and reduces the power of each councilor. Currently, a tie
vote is the only opportunity for the mayor to vote. The existing
odd number of councilors reduces the opportunity for a tie vote.
With an even number of councilors, the chances of a tie vote
would rise and make mayors even more powerful than they are
now.
The proposed Charter amendments are significant, as they
would change the balance of power in city government. There
is no urgency to making these Charter changes.
If you agree with any one of the above three arguments, then
vote NO on Measure 2-159.

Vote No on Measure 2-159
The Charter amendment proposed in this Ballot Measure was
recommended to Council by a Charter Review Task Force led by
the Mayor. Unfortunately, the proposal fails to deliver on three
of the Task Force’s own guiding principles.
Fair and Effective Representation. By deleting the language
in the charter that guides how ward boundaries should be
drawn, this measure makes unfair representation more possible,
not less.
Accountability to Voters and Democratic
Responsiveness. Elections hold councilors accountable.
Extending terms to four years makes council less accountable,
not more.
Accessibility to Elected Leaders and Public Service.
Reducing the number of wards from 9 to 6 means each ward
will be larger for a councilor to walk and will include more
people to represent, resulting in reduced access to elected
leaders.
Students are a significant part of our community and should not
be left out. Longer terms would make it more difficult for
students to run for council, making public service less accessible
to them.
The Task Force argued that these changes would make Council
more efficient. However, the proposal requires ward boundaries
to be redrawn for the second time since the 2020 census. This
is an unneeded waste of time for a new council.
Ten years of eliminating some council advisory committees and
converting others to advising staff has already reduced public
input to comment at meetings with crowded agendas. This
measure goes a step too far, proposing to “streamline”
representation itself.
In Corvallis we need a Council that is more accessible and
responsive to the people not less. Please join us in voting NO on
Measure 2-159!

Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of
city’s annual discretionary budget.
Question: Should Portland create participatory budgeting
program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2%
of city’s discretionary budget?
Summary: Currently, Mayor works with City Administrator,
bureaus, and community to develop proposed budget;
Council then considers, amends as needed and adopts

• Developed with input from oversight committee,

from all Council districts

district projects:

number of feasible projects by city staff
and budget delegates from all districts in a
transparent process
• Feasible projects advance to binding selection
process open, accessible to all residents
• Operational July 2027

City Club of Portland’s Research Finds:
Measure 26-267’s proposed participatory budgeting
approach is “nearly unprecedented” and “difficult to
justify”
Since 1916, City Club of Portland has produced nonpartisan
research to inform voters. On March 15, 2025, after a six-month
study, City Club released a 96-page report on participatory
budgeting (“PB”): Participatory Budgeting for Portland: A City
Club Research Report.
On the exact approach Measure 26-267 takes, City Club’s
conclusion is notable:
“Proposals to adopt and institutionalize PB as a city-wide
program funded through a charter change or citizen initiative
appear to be nearly unprecedented in the U.S. and difficult to
justify from the available evidence about PB’s benefits.”
City Club also found: “municipalities that implement
participatory budgeting rely on its appealing promise rather
than on evidence of its concrete benefits.”
More specifically, City Club found:
Actual participation in participatory budgeting is low
• “Chronically low participation rates... cast doubt on
whether the results of a PB vote actually represent the
true preferences of a community.”
• “Typical participation rates in PB projects are 5% or fewer
of eligible voters.”
Administrative costs are high
• “A consistent finding is the reported high cost of
administering a PB program,” consuming up to 20 percent
or more of the funds set aside in other cities.
A charter-mandated program — like Measure 26-267’s
proposal — “creates unnecessary risks” and diverts tax
dollars from “more strategic purposes”
• “Instituting a PB program that captures a portion of
the general fund, that privileges PB above most other
priorities, and that requires hefty new expenditures for
administration creates unnecessary risks, especially when
the city budget is under such pressure.”
• “With a PB program in place, those funds will be
unavailable for more strategic purposes.”
After this extensive study, City Club recommended a small,
carefully designed pilot — not a permanent charter mandate.
This measure ignores that research. Vote No.

No other city does participatory budgeting the way
Measure 26-267 proposes.
The Measure 26-267 campaign says participatory budgeting
is proven elsewhere, citing New York, Boston, Paris, Seoul, and
Mexico City.
Here’s what they don’t tell you: not one of those cities — not
one city anywhere — has done what this measure would do:
permanently lock a mandatory budget set-aside into its charter.
City Club of Portland’s research committee searched for
precedents. Its conclusion: proposals to institutionalize citywide
participatory budgeting through a charter change are “nearly

unprecedented in the U.S.”
Look at the cities proponents name:
• New York amended its charter in 2018 to require a
program, but there’s no mandatory set-aside.
•
• Boston amended its charter in 2021 to create a
participatory budgeting office, but there’s no mandatory
set-aside.
• Outside the U.S., Paris, Seoul, and Mexico City’s
programs are adjustable when budgets get tight. None
have a mandatory set-aside in their city’s constitution, like
Measure 26-267 proposes.
•
One city did consider the approach in Measure 26-267: In 2023,
Cleveland voters rejected a charter amendment that would
dedicate 2% of their general fund to a participatory budgeting
program.
The closest example may be Seattle, which began with a
$3 million no-bid contract the Washington State Auditor
said showed “only the bare minimum of accountability and
transparency.” Three years passed before a dollar reached the
community. Seattle has about 780,000 residents; only 4,092
people voted. The Seattle Times concluded the $27 million
experiment was “not worth repeating.”
“Everybody’s doing it” is rarely a good argument. But the truth
is, nobody is doing participatory budgeting this way.

No new taxes?
Read the fine print on Measure 26-267.
The Measure 26-267 campaign promises no new taxes, saying
this measure only changes who decides how the money we
already have gets spent.
That’s technically true — and that’s exactly the problem.
Measure 26-267 creates a permanent, mandatory set-aside
(about $16 million dollars to start) written into the city charter,
with no specific funding source. No new revenue. No dedicated
stream of tax dollars. Nothing earmarked to cover this new
program.
This is Budgeting 101. When you create a new funding
obligation with no way to pay for it, one of two things must
happen: Cuts to existing services, or new taxes down the road.
Measure 26-267’s supporters won’t say which one they’d
choose, but it’s a choice we’ll be forced to make.
As for “the money we already have”? Portland doesn’t have it.
The city just closed a record $170 million budget shortfall. It cut
homeless services by $18 million and parks by more than $11
million. Roughly 100 city employees lost their jobs this summer.
There is no extra $16 million. Every dollar in the General Fund is
already paying for firefighters, police officers, 911 dispatchers,
parks maintenance, shelter beds, and other essential city
services. “Changing who decides” how that money gets spent
means taking it away from those services.
Here’s the thing: if this measure really cost nothing, it wouldn’t
need to be locked into the city charter, beyond the reach of
every future mayor and council. You only lock an experimental
program into the charter when you know it couldn’t survive an
honest budget process — where it would have to compete, on
the merits, against fire engines and 911 dispatchers.
A bill with no way to pay it isn’t free. It’s just unpaid. Vote
No on Measure 26-267.
